nlp_justification: Queensland Nature Conservation Legislation Amendment Regulation 2025 — entirely a wildlife/animal licensing amendment (Subordinate Legislation 2025 No. 125). Zero fisheries or marine enforcement relevance. Deals with demerit points, licence grants/renewals for native animal and plant authorities, and protected area camping permits. No VMS/AIS/satellite, no fisheries penalties, no vessel enforcement powers. Score of 10 reflects legislative currency only (2025 publication).

Nova Scotia Fisheries and Coastal Resources Act 1996 (amended to 2021). Genuine fisheries act with strong enforcement chapter (Part IX): explicit inspector powers to board/seize/arrest vessels, corporate offence liability (s.114), forfeiture provisions (s.93), penalties section (s.116), powers of court on conviction (s.115), seizure of fish and property (ss.83/86), additional fines (s.112). Liability assigned to owners and corporate entities. No explicit VMS/AIS/satellite mandates or electronic evidence admissibility provisions visible — technology references limited to scientific databases. Last substantive amendment 2021 (c.31).

Ministerial Accord No. 081 (March 2014) — short 4-page ministerial regulation for jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi) fishery. Strongest feature: Art. 7 explicitly mandates 'Dispositivo de Monitoreo Satelital (DMS)' as permanently operational on all authorized vessels — a direct, specific satellite monitoring requirement. Also mandates fisheries observers on 50% of vessels (Art. 3). Penalties refer back to parent Ley de Pesca without specification (Art. 8). No enforcement powers, no evidence admissibility, no liability framework within this instrument. Currency is 2014 but this is a secondary regulation, not the primary fisheries law.

Fisheries Act of the Maldives, Act No. 14/2019. Comprehensive modern fisheries act with explicit IUU deterrence mandate (Chapter 7, ss.43-44). Chapter 9 (Monitoring Control and Surveillance) grants detailed powers to Police (s.59), Coast Guard (s.60), and Customs (s.61); confiscation and arrest (s.62); forfeiture of foreign vessels (s.67); observer requirements (s.69). Chapter 10 specifies multiple distinct offences with fine-prescribing regulation (s.79). Section 82 (Presumptions) supports evidentiary use of monitoring data. Technology provisions present but left to regulations (s.56). Liability covers owners, operators, masters. Enacted 2019.

New Zealand Maritime Powers Act 2022. Primarily an enforcement/powers act rather than a fisheries statute. Exceptional enforcement authority: explicit boarding (s.18), stopping (s.17), searching (s.20), arrest (s.25), detention of ships (s.23), biometric collection (s.29), hot pursuit doctrine (s.6), forfeiture in certain cases (s.43). Critically, s.6(e) explicitly references satellite tracking in the definition of pursuit: a ship is pursued without interruption even if 'the ship cannot be tracked by radio, radar, satellite, sonar, or any other remote means' — anchoring satellite evidence in legal doctrine. Enforcement officers defined broadly (constables, Customs, Armed Forces, Conservation officers). Limited direct penalty provisions (enforcement powers act). Currency 2022 = maximum score.

Malaysia Merchant Shipping (Oil Pollution) Act 1994 (Act 515). Civil liability act for oil pollution — not a fisheries enforcement law. Strengths: strong strict liability framework for ship owners (s.3), joint and several liability for multiple ships (s.3(3)), limitation of liability provisions (s.6), compulsory insurance requirement (s.11). Penalties exist via civil liability but no criminal fisheries penalties or fines. Evidence admissibility only through standard civil court processes (Surveyor of Ships certification, s.6(3)(c)). No VMS/AIS/satellite provisions. No fisheries-specific enforcement powers. Enacted 1994 with no visible amendments.

Greece Law No. 2516/1997 — industrial and manufacturing installation licensing law. Translator's notes confirm near-zero fisheries relevance. Sole marine connection is Art. 22 petroleum product distribution provisions covering marine fuel (bunkering) for vessels. Penalties are administrative fines (50,000-25,000,000 drachmas) for industrial licensing violations, not fisheries offences (Art. 16). Liability assigned to operators and engineers signing responsible declarations. Inspections by Licensing Authority only. No VMS/AIS/satellite, no vessel boarding powers, no fisheries evidence provisions. 1997 law with no visible amendments.

Chile Ley General de Pesca y Acuicultura (Decreto 430/1992, consolidated to 29-SEP-2025 via Ley 21770). Extremely comprehensive fisheries framework law last amended September 2025. Extensive definitions covering all fishery activities, vessels, quota systems, observers (Art. 26 bis), and catch monitoring. 'Valor de sancion' system (Art. 46) ties penalties explicitly to species tonnage — a sophisticated graduated penalty framework. Satellite monitoring device (DMS) requirements exist via regulations under this act. Subsecretaria de Pesca enforcement powers include vessel inspection, licence suspension, quota enforcement. Liability assigned to 'armadores' (vessel owners), including solidary liability for artisanal fishing communities. Currency score maximum (last modified 2025).

1980 bilateral Spain-Portugal river fishing treaty. No satellite/electronic evidence provisions. Chapter VIII references penalties but no specifics visible. Maritime authorities conduct inspections (Art.6) and vessel owners must provide data (Art.8) but framework is rudimentary. No VMS/AIS. Pre-1990 instrument.

2007 EU-Gabon fisheries access agreement. Not domestic enforcement legislation. No penalty schedule or evidence admissibility rules. Fisheries monitoring provisions vaguely referenced (Art.5.3) but no explicit VMS mandate. Vessel operators subject to Gabonese national law by reference only. 2000-2010 date.

2025 Indonesian regulation on patrol vessel management. Exceptionally strong enforcement authority: stop/board/inspect/detain/hot-pursuit/force powers explicitly codified (Pasal 2-6). VMS centre (pusat pemantauan kapal) and aerial surveillance explicitly mandated as operational support (Pasal 2.3). No penalty schedule or explicit evidence admissibility in pages reviewed. 2025 date.

Italy's general Environmental Code (D.Lgs.152/2006) updated to April 2025. Not fisheries-specific legislation — covers EIA/VAS/water/waste/air/environmental liability. No fisheries enforcement provisions

2001 Mexican emergency technical standard (NOM-EM-04-PESC-2001) on juvenile tuna bycatch in purse-seine fisheries. Sets minimum size and 10% bycatch cap with commercialisation prohibition (Art.4.3). Scientific observer requirement. CONAPESCA compliance evaluation. No VMS/satellite provisions or evidence admissibility rules. Narrow technical instrument.

2023 executive decree implementing Panama's Fisheries Law 204/2021. VMS explicitly defined (Art.6 item 13) and included in national fleet monitoring information system (Art.9). Strong institutional framework (Autoridad de Recursos Acuáticos). Traceability registries established. Applies to all vessel operators including foreign-flagged. No explicit penalty schedule or evidence admissibility provision in pages reviewed.
2003/2004 amendment to South Africa's National Environmental Management Act. Creates detailed environmental management inspector (EMI) system with explicit powers to board vessels
